prime.problem: The sample-killing requirement keeps tests that caught real wrong programs. If those wrong programs include the model you're about to score, the reduced suite is guaranteed to catch it, and "mini is as good as the full suite" becomes true by construction.
prime.fits: Test-suite reduction merged three requirements; this card guards the third. It is the same idea as holding out validation data, applied to models instead of examples.
expect: kills from all models except the one scored
prime.goal: Explain why a model's own kills must be excluded when reducing, trace the procedure on a small kill matrix, and say what leave-one-out still can't guarantee.

attend: Which of the three reduction requirements needs this guard, and why don't the other two?
If GPT-4's own kills were included, what would its mini score be pinned to, and why is that no evidence?
Why build 19 reduced suites instead of one?
What does leave-one-out simulate about a brand-new model, and where does that simulation stop?
Why does full HumanEval+ need none of this?

must: Sample-kill requirements come from models' wrong outputs → including the scored model forces every test that caught it to survive → its reduced score matches the full suite by construction → the validation proves nothing

Exclude the scored model's kills → reduce with the others' only → score it on a suite fitted to other models' mistakes → a gap from the full suite (GPT-4 78.0 vs 76.2) is honest evidence of what mini misses
Each model gets its own reduced suite built from all the others → every suite keeps as much evidence as possible → but the cost is one reduction per model (19)
A released mini is reduced once from a fixed 2023 pool → a new model's unique failure modes may have no catching test → leave-one-out estimates this risk but can't remove it
elevated: Coverage and mutant requirements never look at model outputs → they need no guard → which is also why they give model-independent guarantees for failure modes no model has shown
reference: the 19 models in table 4 vs 26 in table 3
the paper's quote about new LLMs having no execution results

compress.prompt: From memory, write the leave-one-out loop as one line of pseudocode, then explain in 2–3 sentences what circularity it prevents and what risk remains for a model released after mini was built.
checklist: for each model m: reduce using kills from every model except m, then score m
prevents a model's own mistakes from choosing the tests that judge it
without it, mini matches the full suite by construction
a new model's novel failures may not be covered: an estimate, not a guarantee

retrieve.q: Explain the circularity in "reduce using every model's kills, then check that mini ranks the models like the full suite".
answer: the set cover must keep a test for each of a model's recorded wrong samples
so every recorded wrong sample of that model is still caught by mini
agreement with the full suite is then forced, not measured

retrieve.q: Walk through scoring StarCoder-15B with leave-one-out: whose kills build its suite, what is reduced, and what is compared?
answer: kills from all other models in the pool (GPT-4, ChatGPT, CodeGen-16B, …), none from StarCoder
merged with coverage and mutant requirements, then greedy set cover
StarCoder's samples are scored on that suite: 29.3
compared with its full HumanEval+ score (29.3): no gap here

retrieve.q: Would a single split (reduce on half the models, test on the other half) be good enough? What do you gain and lose versus leave-one-out?
answer: lose: each suite sees only half the evidence, so it is weaker
and each model is scored once against one arbitrary split, so noisier

compare.q: Holding out a validation split in training and holding out a model in reduction both avoid the same trap. What is being "fit" in each case, and how does each fail if you skip the hold-out?
answer: training: weights fit to training examples; hold out examples
reduction: the test subset fits to recorded wrong samples; hold out the scored model
skipping it: overfit loss looks great, and mini looks as good as the full suite, both by construction

compare.q: Mutant kills and sample kills are both "tests that caught a bug". Why does only sample killing need leave-one-out?
answer: mutants are generated from the ground truth, independent of any model
sample kills come from the models being evaluated
only the second can leak the scored model's own mistakes into the suite

predict.q: Toy pool: tests t1–t4 and three models, each with one wrong sample. A's is caught only by t4, B's by t1 and t2, C's by t2 and t3. Commit: with leave-one-out, what reduced suite scores A, and does it catch A's wrong sample? What would the circular version keep?
predict.answer: Leave-one-out for A uses B's and C's kills: t2 covers both, so the suite is {t2}, and A's wrong sample passes it: A is over-credited on mini. The circular version must also cover A's sample, so it keeps {t2, t4} and catches it. Leave-one-out exposes that mini would miss A's unique failure; the circular version hides it.

apply.task: Extend the toy: add model D whose wrong sample is caught by t3 and t4. Redo leave-one-out for each of A, B, C and D (greedy, ties broken toward the lower test number). For each model, list its reduced suite and whether it catches that model's wrong sample. Count how many of the four models mini would over-credit.
apply.done: A: the others' samples are B (t1, t2), C (t2, t3), D (t3, t4); greedy takes t2 (B, C) then t3 (D) → {t2, t3}, which misses A (t4 only). B: t3 and t4 tie at 2; t3 (C, D), then t4 (A) → {t3, t4}, misses B. C: t4 (A, D), then t1 (B) → {t1, t4}, misses C. D: t2 (B, C), then t4 (A) → {t2, t4}, catches D. Three of four models are over-credited: with so few models, each one's failure is often unique, which is why the paper's pool of 19 matters.
apply.hint: At each round, count how many still-uncovered wrong samples each test catches.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: A's reduced suite, or which toy models end up over-credited?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why agreement under the circular version proves nothing?
